chapter_theme: Paripadal 15 and 16: Ilamperuvazhuthiyar's hymn to Thirumal at Maalirunkunram, best of hills, where heaven is easily won and the two brothers of different form and one deed are worshipped with kin; and Nalvazhisiyar's Vaiyai song, the flood's coming praised place by place, a feigned bar of menstruation overrun by a lover, the flowered river as the starry sky, and a closing prayer that rain and river never fail.

paripadal:15:1-18.reading: Of the hills that poets have praised, starting from the world-rim mountain that holds the earth, many exist, few among them bring the world its full fruit, fewer still are the clan mountains with clouded peaks, and best of those is this great high hill that bears the two who differ in form but share one deed, joined like the rock cleft and its falls, like word and meaning; heaven is not easy to climb unless the one of the fragrant tulasi grants it, but at Maalirunkunram it is easily won, and that right is what we praise.
paripadal:15:1-18.nuance: The opening narrows like a sieve (பல, then சில, then குல வரை சில, then சிறந்தது) until only one hill is left. Heaven is named twice in two lines: hard to win elsewhere (அரிதின் பெறு துறக்கம்), easy here (எளிதின் பெறல் உரிமை), so the shrine is praised as a shorter road to the same end, and even that road depends on the god's grant (நல்கின் அல்லதை).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of Thirumal's hill as the best of mountains: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the two gods of different form joined in one deed
the two gods of different form joined in one deed

paripadal:15:19-37.reading: The Silambaaru comes down the hill, its swaying falls roaring, as fine as the white kadamba garland on the chest of the god's elder brother whose head is hooded by the snake, and so adorns the hill whose name runs on with Solai, Maalirunkunram, a hill that sows and ripens whatever desire people long for; think, people, how the gold-clad one dwells there joined with his brother, as darkness deepens where the young sunlight mingles with the water, and hear his fragrant fame; with blue lilies open in every spring, asoka in flower on every branch around them, ripe fruit beside unripe and the vengai's bright clusters blooming, the hill has the sweet state of Maayon himself; you who cannot go to worship, look at it and bow: the name Irunkunram has spread, its fame is ancient in the clamouring world, and the god who grants desire takes away confusion from those who see it.
paripadal:15:19-37.nuance: The hill is made to resemble the god twice: its falls are the elder brother's white garland, and its flowering takes on Maayon's own state (மாயோன் ஒத்த). Line 34 lets those who cannot make the journey worship by sight alone (கண்டு பணிமின்), so the hill visible from afar is itself an object of worship. Lines 24 to 28 are compressed and the image of light mingling with dark water may be read of the two brothers or of the hill at dusk.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's hill praised as like the god and as a thing to bow to

comparisons.tenor: the river's falls on the hill

comparisons.vehicle: மன் புனல் இள வெயில் வளாவ இருள் வளர்வென
comparisons.tenor: the gold-clad dark god dwelling joined with his brother

paripadal:15:38-53.reading: The monkey with her young clasped to her leaps from rock to rock, the budding mullai shows the seasons turning in order, the young peahen calls from branches over water clear as gems, leaves fall and the koels call, flute and cymbals play and the singers' practised songs answer the drum, so that the hill's echo never stops: to this dark hill of him who overcame and slew his foes go, with your wives, with your parents, with the infants in your arms and with those you love, honouring the god and bowing toward his quarter; he is the one with eyes like the lotus, his gem-like body mingled with the dark of the rainy night, who appears in whatever world it may be and takes away the suffering when its people are troubled, and who dwells in love on Irunkunram.
paripadal:15:38-53.nuance: The call to pilgrimage names the whole household one by one (wives, parents, infants, loved ones), so the worship is a family journey, not a lone ascetic's. The god's coming is stated in general (எவ்வயின் உலகத்தும் தோன்றி) and his dwelling in particular (இருங்குன்றத்தான்), and the hinge between them is love (அன்பு-அது மேஎய்).

thinai_evidence.note: a call to go and worship the god who removes suffering: paadaan

paripadal:15:54-66.reading: He is named by what he bears: the honeyed fresh tulasi and a form like a dark hill, the bright light and the single earring, the bird on the golden banner, the plough with its strong ring, the club held in anger, the right-whorled conch and the strong discus, the striped bow and its arrows, the disc ringed with bright clusters and the bright sword; since the true sacred word says this is so, and the lord dwells within us and sounds there, we bow and praise the two of great name, asking that we may come to dwell at the feet on Irunkunram.
paripadal:15:54-66.nuance: The litany runs in plurals (-அவை) and mixes the marks of both brothers, the elder's single earring and plough with the younger's tulasi, conch and discus, so the weapons are counted as one possession; only the last line says the praise goes to two (பெரும் பெயர் இருவரை). The god is placed at once on the hill and inside the worshipper (எம் உள் அமர்ந்து இசைத்து), and the prayer asks for the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: closing praise and prayer to the two gods: paadaan

paripadal:16:1-19.reading: The banks, as if copying the giving of a generous-handed lord, wear away everywhere under the pepper and sandal of the dark hill, the foam of curd and much else; at the fords women with darting eyes come crowd after crowd to bathe with their partners, holding their little tufted sons with the munjam on their heads, while pearl strings, pearls from the elephant's brow, gold jewels and gems whirl to the right in the turbid water; the fields, carrying shed flowers and brimming with flower-water, are as lovely as a stage on festival day where dancers trained to the drum's beat perform; the groves give their fragrant narantham, thick with the pollen the bees hum over, as if feasting the sweet flowing water as a guest; in forest groves, ponds and islets the bees drink and sing, and flower-beauty bloomed in every quarter: such is the Vaiyai's coming.
paripadal:16:1-19.nuance: The unit is built on four places, each with its own simile: banks (கரையே), fords (துறையே), fields (செறுவே), groves (காவே). The banks' loss to the flood is praised as giving, and the groves' flowers as a host's welcome, so the river is both the guest that is fed and the cause of a generosity that costs the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's coming praised, the frame of the song: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the banks giving up their goods to the flood
the groves giving flowers to the flood

paripadal:16:20-31.reading: Her companions splash water all round, and a girl who has not wiped the flower-water from her young breasts sees a noble young man coming and presses her thick cloth's hem to herself, while her friends tell him by a lie, 'don't come near, she is in her flowering, go'; they guard her with the scent of cool sandal that looks just like blood and send him off laughing; but he, like a river rushing on to the great sea, does not hold back, leaves the heady honeyed wine, comes close without wiping away the red, and embraces her sweetly, so that their cry 'the lady has flowered, hail!' turned to shame: such is the Vaiyai's coming.
paripadal:16:20-31.nuance: The friends use the bar of menstruation (பூத்தனள்) to keep a lover off, with red sandal standing in for blood; he ignores the bar, and the same word comes back as a joke (பூத்தனள் நங்கை; பொலிக). Whose shame line 30 means, the girl's or the lying friends', is not fixed by the text. The refrain வையை வரவு makes the scene part of the flood's arrival.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover breaks through a feigned bar to embrace the girl at the river

comparisons.tenor: the young man pressing on undeterred

paripadal:16:32-38.reading: The falls coming down from the hill join the bank trees beside the groves full of clusters and grow lovely, and the cool buds from the women's hair and the petals slipped from the men's flowered chests spread over the water, so that the Vaiyai, humming with bees, always looks like the sky where the wide Ganga of the heavens, flowered with stars, has passed.
paripadal:16:32-38.nuance: The stars are said to flower (மீன் ஆரம் பூத்த), so the simile runs both ways: flowers on the river are stars, and the stars of the heavenly river are flowers. The flowers are the lovers' castoffs, so the river's sky is made of the night's adornments.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's constant beauty praised: paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: மீன் ஆரம் பூத்த வியன் கங்கை நந்திய வானம்
comparisons.tenor: the river strewn with fallen flowers

paripadal:16:39-47.reading: In toddy, in water and in sulking, these three, the women's bright kohl-lined eyes, red-streaked like kendai fish, with bee swarms circling their mouths and honey dripping where the flowers fall, the bathers who plunge again and again in the deep water are embraced, and the man whose chest is smeared with musk paste and marked with scars yields to them; the sight is like a hill where a hanging honeycomb drips when bent bamboo springs up and strikes it: such is the nature of the Vaiyai of the king of the bannered chariot.
paripadal:16:39-47.nuance: The three in which the eyes redden, toddy, water and the sulk, set drink, bathing and quarrel side by side as one play. The closing simile makes the embrace a sudden release, as the bamboo springs back and the honey falls. The syntax of lines 40 to 44 is loose, and who embraces whom can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: lovers embrace at the river after drink and sulking

paripadal:16:48-55.reading: Clouds roar on the hills and this sweet water roars in waves on the banks; so that those who wear chaplets, chest garlands and fragrant hair garlands may take by bathing, day after day, the fruit of the gifts they have made, may the sky never refuse to keep the rain, the fragrant sandal, the garlands, the flowering smoke and the offerings from drying, and may your flood swell and never run dry, Vaigai.
paripadal:16:48-55.nuance: The prayer ties rite to rain: the sky is asked not to let the offerings dry (புலராமை), and bathing in the river is when the giver collects the fruit of past giving (பண்ணிய ஈகைப் பயன்). The river is addressed directly only in the last word, நினக்கு.

thinai_evidence.note: closing prayer to sky and river: paadaan

links.note: Paripadal 13.10-13 says the god's chest holds by right (உரிமை) the heaven of those who worship it; Paripadal 15.15-18 says heaven is hard to climb unless the tulasi-wearer grants it, but is gained easily, by right (உரிமை), at Maalirunkunram.
links.teaches: The same claim of a worshipper's right to heaven is lodged first in the god's body and then in a hill one can walk to, so the pair shows Thirumal's grace being given a place on the map near Madurai.

links.note: Paripadal thirattu 12 says those who live in Koodal and Parankunram are the ones truly living, and asks who would go to the world of the gods; Paripadal 15.15-18 keeps heaven as the goal and praises Maalirunkunram as the easy way to it.
links.teaches: One Madurai poet makes the sacred hill a substitute that makes heaven unwanted and another makes it a means to heaven, so the shrine hills could be praised either as better than the world above or as its gate.

links.note: Paripadal 1.1-13 describes two forms in turn, the white one with the hooded heads, the curved plough and a single earring, then the dark one with the bird banner; Paripadal 15.54-61 lists the single earring, the ringed plough, the tulasi, conch, discus and bird banner in one run of plurals and worships them as the two of great name.
links.teaches: Song 1 keeps the brothers' marks apart in two portraits, while song 15 pours them into one litany and addresses the pair, so together they show the Balarama and Krishna emblems hardening into a shared catalogue of one double deity.

links.note: Paripadal 13.22-36 makes the plough-bearer one of three forms of a single god (மூஉரு ஆகிய தலைபிரி ஒருவனை); Paripadal 15 keeps them as two, different in form but one in deed (வேறு வேறு உருவின் ஒரு தொழில் இருவர்), and bows to the two.
links.teaches: Against song 13's solution, which absorbs the brother as a form of the one god, song 15 keeps two persons and finds their unity in a single deed, like word and meaning, so the Paripadal holds two theologies of the pair.

links.note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere at any time; Paripadal 15.49-53 says the god appears in whatever world and removes suffering when people are troubled, and sends worshippers with their families to his hill.
links.teaches: The Kural puts the movement on the devotee who reaches the feet, while the hymn puts it on a god who comes into each world and on the pilgrim's journey to one hill, so release from suffering is framed as both an inward arrival and a visit.

links.note: Kural 18 warns that if the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods; Paripadal 16.48-55 prays that the sky never refuse, so that the sandal, garlands, smoke and offerings of the river festival never dry and the Vaigai never runs dry.
links.teaches: The Kural states the dependence of worship on rain as a general warning, and the hymn turns the same dependence into a prayer said at the festival it describes, so the couplet's rule is shown at work in the Vaigai rites.

links.note: Paripadal 12.81-83 has the settled Vaiyai show heaven's beauty as a reflection in its water; Paripadal 16.32-38 makes the flood itself look like the sky through which the star-flowered heavenly Ganga runs, with the lovers' fallen flowers as its stars.
links.teaches: One poet finds the sky in the clear river after the flood and another in the flood's floating flowers, so the pair shows the Vaiyai as heaven on earth being made both from stillness and from festival litter.

links.note: Kural 215 likens the wealth of a wise man who helps the world to the village tank filled with water; Paripadal 16.1-4 likens the banks, worn away as the flood carries off pepper, sandal and curd foam, to the giving of a generous lord.
links.teaches: The Kural uses full water as the image of a giver's wealth, and the Paripadal uses a giver as the image of water taking from its banks, so the pair shows the river-and-giving figure running both ways, with the Paripadal stressing that giving is a wearing away.

source_issues: Paripadal 15 and 16: the colophons have no thinai or thurai; only the subject (திருமால், வையை), the poets, the music and the pan நோதிறம் are given.

Paripadal 15 lines 19 and 35 are flagged as dropped modern headings; both read as verse in context (the elder brother's garland simile; the spread of the name Irunkunram) and are marked as verse. Line 23 had ொ restored and line 64 was repaired from sangamtamil.com (flags); line 39 is not in sangamtamil.com.

Paripadal 15 line 11, கல் அறை கடாம் கானலும், is obscure; read as the rock cleft and its falls, a pair joined like word and meaning. Lines 24 to 28 (தாம் வீழ் காமம் ... புணஎந்து அமர் நிலையே) are compressed; line 28 புணஎந்து is read as புணர்ந்து.

Paripadal 16 lines 20, 33 and 50 are flagged as dropped modern headings; all three read as verse. Line 26 had ொ restored (flag); lines 2 and 3 had யொடு restored by rule and are not confirmed by sangamtamil.com.
Paripadal 16 line 29 prints மரு(வ) with a bracketed editorial letter. Lines 40 to 45 are hard to construe; the subject of புல்ல and குழைந்து is uncertain. Line 7 திணை பிரி புதல்வர் is obscure.
